children.text: A volcano whose summit collapsed in one of the 20th century's largest eruptions in
, leaving a caldera now filled with an emerald-green lake. Ride a 4x4 jeep across a canyon of hardened volcanic ash (lahar), then trek up a riverbed to look down over the crater lake.
Mount Pinatubo is a stratovolcano rising at the border of Tarlac, Zambales, and Pampanga provinces. Dormant for over 500 years, it erupted on
in what became the second-largest terrestrial volcanic eruption of the 20th century. The eruption caused the entire summit to collapse, lowering the mountain's height from about
above sea level to around
, and creating a massive caldera roughly
2.5km
across. Ash and sulfur dioxide that shot up into the stratosphere had a global effect, cooling the Earth's average temperature by about 0.5°C over the following one to two years.

The Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) and the U.S. Geological Survey (USGS), which had been tracking the earthquakes and steam explosions that continued for more than two months before the eruption, warned of the major eruption in advance, and about 60,000 residents within a
30km
radius of the volcano were evacuated before
June 15
. On that same day, however, Typhoon Yunya (known locally as Diding) struck, and rain-soaked ash collapsed roofs, killing 847 people. The ash column rose to a height of about
35km
, and for years afterward, every time it rained, lahars poured down the rivers; in
San Guillermo Church, Bacolor
was buried to half its height. Clark Air Base, the U.S. Air Force base blanketed in ash, became today's
Clark
Freeport Zone after the U.S. military left.

After the eruption, rainwater collected in the caldera to form today's Pinatubo crater lake. The water, laced with dissolved volcanic minerals, shifts between emerald, teal, and jade depending on the sunlight, standing out vividly against the grey cliffs that surround it. The route to the lake is itself spectacular. The vast grey sand plains and canyons carved dozens of meters deep, formed as ash and debris flows (lahar) from the eruption hardened, look like a scene from another planet.

The Pinatubo area is home to the Aeta, one of the indigenous peoples of the Philippines. The eruption wiped out many Aeta villages and forced people to relocate; today they make a living by taking part in 4x4 driving, guiding, and tourism services. The Aeta have long regarded the mountain as the dwelling place of the god Apo Namalyari, and in
January 2010
the National Commission on Indigenous Peoples (NCIP) recognized about 15,984 hectares on the Zambales side, including the summit and the lake, as Aeta ancestral domain.

The route most travelers use starts from Sta. Juliana in Capas, Tarlac, riding a 4x4 across the lahar fields before hiking up along a riverbed. The physical demands are moderate, so even those without much hiking experience can manage it comfortably, making it a good recommendation for travelers interested in geology and natural history, or for expats who want to give family or guests visiting from home a special day out.
Ride a jeep for about
1–1.5 hours
from Sta. Juliana across the ash plains around Crow Valley and the O'Donnell River. Crossing waterways and cresting sand dunes is a thrilling experience in itself.
From the 4x4 drop-off point, you hike about
3–7km
up to the crater in
1–2 hours

. The walking distance depends on how far the 4x4s can get in on the day. Most of the trail is gently sloping sand and gravel, with several shallow stream crossings. Walking between giant boulders and sheer volcanic ash cliffs is the highlight of the scenery.
Look down over the caldera lake from the viewpoint at the end of the trek. The water shows its most vivid emerald color around
10 AM
, when the sunlight is strong.
You can see textbook volcanic terrain firsthand: spots where steam rises and sulfur can be smelled, layered ash cross-sections, and massive boulders flung out during the eruption.

blocks.title: Meet an Aeta village and its culture

children.text: On the way, you'll pass through an Aeta community village, where an indigenous guide can share stories about the eruption. Be respectful and ask permission before taking photos.

blocks.title: Volcanic sand bath at Puning Hot Spring

children.text: To reach Puning Hot Spring in Sapang Bato, Angeles, you ride a 4x4 for
45 minutes–1 hour

through a canyon piled with Pinatubo ash; there you can enjoy lahar sand baths warmed by geothermal heat, mud packs, and hot spring soaks. There are 11 hot spring pools, and tours from Clark cost about
per person based on a group of four or more; you can't get in without a reservation. It's a great way to recover the day after the trek.

blocks.title: Climbing to the crater ridge via the Inararo route

children.text: A new route that enters by 4x4 from Inararo village in Porac, Pampanga, and climbs about
5.8km

one way past Ana-an Falls. It is harder than the Capas route, with many sections of scrambling over rocks and crossing streams, but you can look down on the lake from the crater ridge, and foreigners can join without an Air Force visit permit.

blocks.title: Climbing from the Zambales side via the Botolan route

children.text: In Botolan, Zambales, where the crater itself lies, 4x4s leave Camp Kainomayan near the Bucao River at
6 AM
and spend about
2 hours
crossing lahar rivers and sand dunes, after which you walk about
3km
to reach the lake. It runs only in the dry season,
January–May
, and the starting point has a stream play area, a swimming pool, and showers.

With steeper climbs and more rock scrambling than the Capas route, it suits experienced hikers. Foreigners can go without an Air Force visit permit, but age limits and booking deadlines vary by operator, so check in advance.

Walk-in visitors without a reservation are not accepted, and the road into Station 1 is narrow and steep, making it hard to reach by public transport.
From Manila, take NLEX up and switch to SCTEX, then exit at Concepcion and head toward Capas. From Capas town, it's about
20km
of country road west to Sta. Juliana. It takes about
3–3.5 hours
from Manila, or about
1–1.5 hours
from Clark. There's parking around the Sta. Juliana registration office.

Even if you go independently without a tour package, you book in advance with a local-government-accredited 4x4 operator in Sta. Juliana and register at the Capas tourism office. A 4x4 (up to 5 people) costs
plus a
guide fee, and adding the
tourism fee and
Botolan fee per person brings the total to
for one person or
for five (
each).
From Cubao or Pasay, take a bus bound for Tarlac City, Baguio, or Dagupan (Victory Liner, Five Star, etc.) and get off in front of McDonald's in Capas (Capas Junction). It takes about
2.5–3 hours
and costs about
. From Capas to Sta. Juliana, a tricycle or chartered vehicle takes about
40 minutes–1 hour
and costs about
per vehicle. Making the pre-dawn registration means catching a bus in the middle of the night, which isn't easy, so a tour package is the realistic option for travelers using public transport.

Clark International Airport (CRK), with direct flights from Korea, is the closest. It's most convenient to stay in Clark or Angeles and take a pre-dawn pickup tour. Tours departing from Clark or Manila, bundling transport, 4x4, guide, entrance fee, and lunch, are sold for about
per person.
Asiana Airlines, Jeju Air, and Jin Air fly daily to Clark from Incheon, Jin Air from Busan, and Aero K from Cheongju (based on the airport flight schedule as of
October 2026
; schedules change by season). From Clark airport to Sta. Juliana is about
1 hour
by car.
Joiner tours, where several travelers share one van, leave Manila at around
2–3 AM
and return in the evening. They cost about

per person, including the round-trip van, tolls, registration fee, Botolan fee, and guide; meals and shower fees are paid separately. Many packages only depart once 11–14 people have signed up for a van, so check the booking conditions.
It takes about
1–1.5 hours
by 4x4 from SM City Clark to the parking point in Inararo village, Porac. Regular vehicles can't get through the lahar roads, so the only way in is an operator's 4x4 pickup tour.
From Cubao, Pasay, or Caloocan in Manila, take a Victory Liner bus bound for Iba or Santa Cruz and get off at Botolan. It's about
4.5–5 hours
to Iba, with fares of
, and Botolan comes just before Iba. Book the 4x4 through the Botolan tourism office; packages including the 4x4, guide, and environmental fee run about
per person.
Peak season is the dry season,
December–April
December–February
has cool dawns and clear skies, when the lake's water looks its most beautiful.
March–April
has clear skies too, but the lahar plains reflect the sun so strongly that the midday heat index can reach 40°C, making an early start and plenty of water essential.
During the
June–October

wet season, upstream rain can swell the lahar river in an instant, and with the risk of debris flows, tours are often suspended or closed for extended periods. When a typhoon warning or heavy rain is forecast, authorities ban entry, so a wet-season visit isn't recommended.
November
and
May
sit on the boundary between dry and wet seasons, so it's best to decide flexibly based on the weather.

Pinatubo is still classified as an active volcano. If the Philippine Institute of Volcanology and Seismology (PHIVOLCS) raises the alert level, entry is immediately restricted, so check the alert status before you set off.
The Capas route had all tourism suspended from
over an issue of ancestral domain rights of the Aeta community, and reopened on

. Also, Crow Valley, which the 4x4s pass through, is an Air Force firing range, so trekking is sometimes halted for several days during the annual spring US-Philippine joint exercise (Balikatan). If you are going in spring, be sure to check with the tour operator before departing whether it is operating.

The most realistic way to make the pre-dawn registration is to stay the night before in Clark or Angeles. The Clark Freeport Zone and Angeles area offer everything from budget-to-midrange hotels at about
a night to resort-style hotels at
or more, and it's about
1–1.5 hours
by car from Clark to Sta. Juliana. There are also modest lodges and homestays around Capas and Sta. Juliana, so arriving and staying the night before lets you start out with the most ease.

There's no shop along the trek, so bring snacks and water. On the way back, be sure to try the food of Pampanga, known as the "culinary capital of the Philippines." Angeles is the birthplace of sisig, chopped pig's head sizzled on a hot plate, and the old restaurants known as its originators are still thriving. Burong kanin, a tangy fermented rice side dish, and tocino, sweet cured pork, are also Pampanga's pride.
Aling Lucing's on Glaciano Valdez Street in Angeles is known as the place where, in
, Lucia Cunanan created today's sisig by grilling and chopping pig's ears and cheeks and serving them on a sizzling hot plate; it also has branches in Clark and elsewhere. Every
December
, Angeles holds a sisig festival.
The registration cutoff is set for an early pre-dawn hour. Being late may make same-day entry impossible, so be sure to keep to your tour operator's meeting time.
There are many stream crossings along the trekking section. Wear trekking sandals that can get wet, or quick-drying running shoes.
The 4x4 section is very dusty with volcanic ash. Bring a mask or buff and sunglasses, and keep your camera in a ziplock bag.
Bring at least 2 liters of water per person, electrolyte drinks, and energy bars. Long stretches have almost no shade, so fluid loss is high.
A wide-brimmed hat, a long-sleeve rash guard, and sunscreen are essential. The lahar sand reflects sunlight, and your face and neck can burn easily.
Photos of the lake come out most vivid around
. The water looks murky when it's cloudy, so wait a bit at the viewpoint if needed.
The registration office accepts cash only. Withdraw money in advance at an ATM in Capas town.
A tip for the 4x4 driver and guide (about
per person) isn't required, but it's customary.

Those aged 60 and over should bring a paper medical certificate saying they are fit to hike or a travel insurance policy covering outdoor activities, and children are accepted only from age 6 or 7 depending on the operator. Those aged 40–59 may have their blood pressure taken on site.

Since the reopening, the Capas route is in principle booked only through operators accredited by the local government. Before booking, check whether the tour fee includes the 4x4, guide, environmental fee, and Botolan fee.
Swimming and boating in the crater lake are prohibited. Because there are no lifeguards at the lakeshore and the water gets deep suddenly near the edge, swimming has been banned since
January 2013
, so even if you go down to the lakeshore, don't go into the water.
Foreigners need a Philippine Air Force (PAF) visit permit to take the Capas route.
You must submit your passport photo page through an accredited operator at least 35 days before your visit

, and if you go without a permit, you will be turned back at the registration desk. This applies to travelers of every nationality, so if your schedule is tight, consider the Inararo route, which needs no permit.
During the wet season or right after rain, the lahar rivers can rise suddenly. If your guide tells you to turn back, follow the instruction immediately. In
August 2009
, typhoon-driven heavy rain swelled the O'Donnell River, and five people, including tourists and a guide who had gotten out of their 4x4 to cross the river, died; in
August 2026
, PHIVOLCS again warned that heavy southwest monsoon rains could send lahars down the O'Donnell and other rivers around Pinatubo.
The stairs and path down to the lakeshore are sometimes closed or restricted depending on the period. Don't go past the safety line at the viewpoint.
Always hold onto the handrail while the 4x4 is moving, and don't lean your body outside the vehicle. The jolts are severe on rough sections.
Heatstroke and dehydration at midday are the most common incidents. If you have a cardiovascular condition or are older, don't push yourself, and rest well partway through.
When passing through an Aeta community village, don't hand out candy or money to children indiscriminately. If you want to help, use an official community program instead.
About
1–1.5 hours
by car. A hub city for the airport, resorts, the hot air balloon festival, and Kapampangan food trips.
About
40 minutes
by car. A memorial obelisk built on the site of Camp O'Donnell, where countless prisoners died at the end of the Bataan Death March.
About
2 hours
by car. A former U.S. naval base where you can enjoy jungle experiences, a marine theme park, and beaches.
About
3 hours
by car. A camping spot in Zambales with a grey sand beach formed by Pinatubo's ash and a grove of agoho trees.
About
1.5 hours
by car. A Spanish-era church buried by lahar in 1995 to roughly half of its 12m height; what were once its second-floor windows now serve as the entrance.
